land.text: the coast and Northern Peru, 'under republican command' (Protectorate of Peru page): Tumbes, Piura, Lambayeque, La Libertad, Cajamarca, Amazonas, Ancash, Lima and Ica; Lima is confidence 3, the departments of the north and the Ica coast are my reading (confidence 2); Callao (Real Felipe) is left out

predecessors.note: San Martin proclaimed independence at Lima on 28 July 1821 (the royalists had left Lima on 25 June); 'the coast and Northern Peru were under republican command, but the rest of the country was controlled by the royalists' (Protectorate of Peru page), so the republic's land is the coast and the north, not a circle round Lima. The royalist highlands and the south stayed Spanish until Ayacucho (9 December 1824) and Callao until 23 January 1826 (Spanish Empire dossier). The spanish-empire dossier's 1821-07 loss (Lima, 120 km) must be widened to this region.

capitals.name: Lima
capitals.note: Infobox capital: Lima. During the Peru-Bolivian Confederation (1836-1839) the Confederation's own capital was Tacna; Lima was occupied by Chile from January 1881 to 29 October 1883.

correction.text: the coast and Northern Peru, 'under republican command' (Protectorate of Peru page): Tumbes, Piura, Lambayeque, La Libertad, Cajamarca, Amazonas, Ancash, Lima and Ica; Lima is confidence 3, the departments of the north and the Ica coast are my reading (confidence 2); Callao (Real Felipe) is left out

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe: Peruvian independence was declared at Lima on 28 July 1821 (Peru page: Lima occupied 12 July). The Protectorate of Peru page says 'the coast and Northern Peru were under republican command, but the rest of the country was controlled by the royalists' (capital Cuzco); it names no department, so the coast and the north are drawn as Tumbes, Piura, Lambayeque, La Libertad, Cajamarca, Amazonas, Ancash, Lima and Ica (Lima confidence 3, the north confidence 2; Pisco and Ica were republican from September 1820). Maynas (Loreto) is not on the page and joins with the rest in December 1824; Callao (Real Felipe) is left out. This replaces an earlier 120 km circle round Lima that the reviewer found far too small.

correction.text: the coast and Northern Peru, 'under republican command' (Protectorate of Peru page): Tumbes, Piura, Lambayeque, La Libertad, Cajamarca, Amazonas, Ancash, Lima and Ica; Lima is confidence 3, the departments of the north and the Ica coast are my reading (confidence 2); Callao (Real Felipe) is left out

keyframe_review.note: 1.47 M km2 against the infobox 1.285 M km2 (modern area, ratio 1.14). The shape draws nearly all of Peru as republican from 1822 (plus Peru-claimed Brazilian Amazon, 1,211 cells, and Chilean Tarapaca and Arica), but the Protectorate of Peru page has the republic hold only 'the coast and Northern Peru' while 'the rest of the country was controlled by the royalists' (capital Cuzco) until Ayacucho on 9 December 1824; the shape is therefore cut to the coast and north (about 0.25 M km2; the departments are my reading, confidence 2, Lima 3). The page gives no territorial change inside 1822-1824: Ica fell to a royalist incursion in April 1822 and Republicans lost at Torata and Moquegua in January 1823 (Protectorate page), and the royalists re-entered Lima on 25 February 1824 after the Callao mutiny of 5 February (Second siege of Callao page), but the pages give no date for the republic's return, so those swings are not drawn (gap). The Brazilian Amazon cells, which Cliopatria gives to its Bolivia shape from 1825, are dropped.

Cliopatria's 1.13 M km2 shape is Peru after Ayacucho, without the Amazon land that went to Bolivia, without Callao (Spanish until 23 January 1826, when the fortress was handed over; its cells appear in the 1828 shape, +7) and without Tumbes, Jaen and Maynas, which it gives to Gran Colombia until 1834. The Gran Colombia-Peru War page calls them 'Peruvian territories' that Gran Colombia only claimed ('claims ... dating from colonial times'), reports no Gran Colombian occupation of them, and the armistice 'recognized' them as Peruvian; the Spanish Empire dossier already gives Peru all of Peru in December 1824. They are added here (adjust) by using the 1834 shape, whose Maynas reaches the equator (bbox -0.1 against -3.3), i.e. beyond modern Loreto, which the ledger and the contest zone only proxy; the land is contested with gran-colombia until 1829. The Ayacucho date is on the Peru page; the 1825 Amazon loss to Bolivia is on no page opened (Bolivia-Peru relations, opened on the reviewer's suggestion, is silent; Bolivia-Peru border returned 404).

correction.text: Peru after Ayacucho with Tumbes, Jaen and Maynas, drawn as Cliopatria's 1834 shape (which adds them, +824 cells, with Maynas reaching the equator): the pages call them 'Peruvian territories' that Gran Colombia claimed, and the Armistice of Piura only 'recognized' them (contest from 1822 to 10 July 1829)

the 1828 shape (1828-1833) with Tumbes, Jaen and Maynas added, i.e. Cliopatria's 1834 shape applied to the whole span; they are Peruvian throughout, contested by Gran Colombia until the Armistice of Piura (10 July 1829)

keyframe_review.note: The 1828 shape (1.14 M km2, valid in Cliopatria 1828-1833) lacks Tumbes, Jaen and Maynas, which it adds only in 1834 (+824 cells). The Gran Colombia-Peru War page says the Armistice of Piura of 10 July 1829 'recognized Tumbes, Jaen and Maynas as Peruvian territories' and the Larrea-Gual Treaty of 22 September 1829 kept the status quo ante bellum: the land was Peruvian before the war and only claimed by Gran Colombia, so the provinces are added for the whole span and the contest events (1822 to July 1829) carry the Gran Colombian claim. This replaces the earlier new 1829-1833 keyframe, which became redundant.

1.37 M km2 (infobox 1.285 M km2, modern, ratio 1.07): the Peru that holds Tumbes, Jaen and Maynas (Loreto, Cajamarca and Amazonas shares, plus slivers of Ecuador's and Colombia's Amazon) and, in the south, Tarapaca and Arica. Valid 1834-1835; Cliopatria has no Peru shape for 1836-1839, the Peru-Bolivian Confederation covers those years.
Identical to the 1834 shape (1.37 M km2): Peru restored after Yungay (20 January 1839) and the Confederation's dissolution; the North and South Peruvian states were absorbed back.

1.365 M km2: the 1840 shape without 29 cells of Brazilian Amazon (and one of Colombia's). The page opened (Brazil-Peru border) gives only the 1909 Treaty of Rio de Janeiro; the 1853 change is unverified: page silent.

correction.text: Peru before the war, with the occupied departments still Peruvian

keyframe_review.note: 1.25 M km2: Cliopatria removes Tarapaca, Arica, Tacna, Moquegua and parts of Puno, Lima and Ica in 1880. The page dates the Chilean occupation of Tarapaca to November 1879, Tacna and Arica to May-June 1880 and Lima to January 1881, but cedes only Tarapaca, in the Treaty of Ancon (20 October 1883). Peru keeps its pre-war shape (the 1853 shape, 1.37 M km2) for 1880-1882, with the Chilean occupations as hatched events; the page says Chile only 'planned to retain Moquegua' and 'the occupation of Arequipa and Puno ... saw little military action' (undated). Added after review: Moquegua (the page: Chile 'planned to retain' it; no occupation date), Arequipa (occupied on 29 October 1883 when Peruvian troops mutinied against Montero and 'allowed the Chileans to occupy the city') and Puno (a march 'to Arequipa and Puno in October 1883') are hatched by occupation events with republic-of-chile; the page gives no end dates, so they end with the last Chilean embarkation at Callao on 4 August 1884.

correction.text: Peru's sovereign land with Tacna and Arica kept in it: the Treaty of Ancon gave Chile only 'temporary control' (War of the Pacific infobox) and the Tacna-Arica page says they 'had been administered by Chile since 1883' until the 1929 treaty; they are drawn Peruvian and hatched by the occupation events

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe 1883-1884: Tarapaca ceded to Chile ('Peru formally cede Tarapaca to Chile', Treaty of Ancon, 20 October 1883); Tacna and Arica remain Peruvian under ten years of Chilean control; Lima is evacuated on 29 October 1883 and the Chilean forces sail from Callao on 4 August 1884. Arequipa (from 29 October 1883) and Puno (October 1883) are also occupied, and Moquegua still (since 1880), until the embarkation of 4 August 1884; see the ledger.

correction.text: Peru's sovereign land with Tacna and Arica kept in it: the Treaty of Ancon gave Chile only 'temporary control' (War of the Pacific infobox) and the Tacna-Arica page says they 'had been administered by Chile since 1883' until the 1929 treaty; they are drawn Peruvian and hatched by the occupation events

keyframe_review.note: 1.30 M km2: the Cliopatria shape has Moquegua, Puno, Lima and Ica back (the Chilean evacuation of 1884) but only 14 percent of Tacna and none of Arica, i.e. it gives them to Chile. The page says Tacna and Arica 'had been administered by Chile since 1883' under a plebiscite clause for 1893 that 'never took place', and that Chile 'retained its sovereignty over Arica' only by the Treaty of Lima of 3 June 1929; they stay Peruvian here, hatched. Tarata, inside Tacna, was administered by Chile from 1880 and returned to Peru on 1 September 1925 (Tarata Province page); it is hatched until then.

correction.text: Peru's sovereign land with Tacna and Arica kept in it: the Treaty of Ancon gave Chile only 'temporary control' (War of the Pacific infobox) and the Tacna-Arica page says they 'had been administered by Chile since 1883' until the 1929 treaty; they are drawn Peruvian and hatched by the occupation events

keyframe_review.note: As the 1885 shape. Cliopatria adds 26 Tacna cells in 1926: they are Tarata, which the Tarata Province page says Chilean troops occupied in 1880 and Chile administered 'from 1880 to 1925' until its return to Peru on 1 September 1925 (ledger: occupation_end 1925-09, mirroring republic-of-chile /ledger/33); the Tacna-Arica compromise page is silent on Tarata and on the 1925 award. Tacna and Arica (less Tarata) stay in Peru's sovereign shape under Chilean administration until 1929.

correction.text: Peru's sovereign land with Tacna and Arica kept in it: the Treaty of Ancon gave Chile only 'temporary control' (War of the Pacific infobox) and the Tacna-Arica page says they 'had been administered by Chile since 1883' until the 1929 treaty; they are drawn Peruvian and hatched by the occupation events

keyframe_review.note: Leticia leaves the shape in 1928 (Colombia gains 30 cells of Amazonas): the Salomon-Lozano Treaty, signed on 24 March 1922, was approved by the Peruvian Congress on 20 December 1927 and took effect on 19 March 1928; the page says only that the act of transfer was signed in 1930 and gives no handover date. Tacna and Arica added as in the 1885 shape.
1.30 M km2: after the Treaty of Lima of 3 June 1929 'Tacna was awarded to Peru' and Chile 'retained its sovereignty over Arica'; the shape holds 95 percent of Tacna and none of Arica.

Identical to the 1929 shape except one cell (Tumbes 0.88 against 0.81): the Ecuadorian-Peruvian War of 1941 and the Rio Protocol of 29 January 1942 left Peru's shape as it was; Peru withdrew from El Oro on 12 February 1942.

1.303 M km2 against the infobox 1.285 M km2 (Peru page, ratio 1.01). Stable to the Cenepa War of 1995 and the Brasilia Presidential Act of 26 October 1998, which the Ecuador page calls the 'definitive peace agreement'.

region.text: the coast and Northern Peru, 'under republican command' (Protectorate of Peru page): Tumbes, Piura, Lambayeque, La Libertad, Cajamarca, Amazonas, Ancash, Lima and Ica; Lima is confidence 3, the departments of the north and the Ica coast are my reading (confidence 2); Callao (Real Felipe) is left out

ledger.note: 1821: San Martin proclaims Peruvian independence at Lima on 28 July 1821; the royalists had left the city on 25 June and the expedition entered two days later. 'The coast and Northern Peru were under republican command, but the rest of the country was controlled by the royalists.' Lima is confidence 3; the nine departments are my reading of 'the coast and Northern Peru' (the page names none of them), hence confidence 2. Callao is left out. Second page (Peru): 'declared Peruvian independence on 28 July 1821' after occupying Lima on 12 July; Protector decree of 3 August 1821. Cliopatria's Republic of Peru begins in 1822.

region.text: Tumbes, Jaen and Maynas, claimed by Gran Colombia and recognised as Peruvian territories by the Armistice of Piura

ledger.note: 1822: Gran Colombia's claim on Tumbes, Jaen and Maynas. The page speaks of 'Gran Colombian claims on the Peruvian territories of Jaen and Maynas' 'dating from colonial times' and reports no occupation of them by either side; the year is Cliopatria's (its Gran Colombia shape holds the land from 1822) and mirrors gran-colombia /ledger/4. Tumbes and Jaen are Peruvian from 1821 in this dossier; the Maynas (Loreto) part joins Peru only in December 1824 (spanish-empire), so before then it is a claim, not held land.

minus.text: the coast and Northern Peru, 'under republican command' (Protectorate of Peru page): Tumbes, Piura, Lambayeque, La Libertad, Cajamarca, Amazonas, Ancash, Lima and Ica; Lima is confidence 3, the departments of the north and the Ica coast are my reading (confidence 2); Callao (Real Felipe) is left out

region.text: the royalist highlands, the south and Maynas: the adjusted 1825 shape (with Tumbes, Jaen and Maynas) minus the coast and north the republic already held

ledger.note: 1824: Ayacucho frees the highlands. The battle of 9 December 1824 was 'decisive', 'consolidating the independence of Peru and Upper Peru'. The extent is the Spanish Empire dossier's royalist highlands and south (all of Peru less Lima); the page does not name them. The remainder is the 1825 shape (with Maynas) minus the coast and north held since 1821 (/ledger/0), so the 1824 gain is the part held by the royalists. Callao and its fortress stayed Spanish to 1826.

1826: Callao surrenders. After the mutiny of 5 February 1824 the garrison of Real Felipe joined the royalists; in January 1825 Rodil 'rejected the surrender proposal'; 'negotiations began with General Salom on January 11, 1826 and concluded with the handover of the fortress on January 23.'

region.text: Guayaquil, held by Peru until 21 July 1829

ledger.note: 1829: Peru holds Guayaquil. 'The city finally surrendered on 19 January 1829'; the Peruvian navy had attacked its defences on 22-24 November 1828.

region.text: Loja (Saraguro, 13 February 1829) and the Cuenca highlands (Portete de Tarqui, 26-27 February 1829)

ledger.note: 1829: Peru invades the south of Gran Colombia. 'Seized the city of Loja by winning the Battle of Saraguro on the 13 February 1829'; Portete de Tarqui, 26-27 February, 'was not decisive'.

region.text: Loja (Saraguro, 13 February 1829) and the Cuenca highlands (Portete de Tarqui, 26-27 February 1829)

ledger.note: 1829: the fighting stops. 'On the 28 February 1829, La Mar and Sucre signed a conditioning document.'

region.text: Tumbes, Jaen and Maynas, claimed by Gran Colombia and recognised as Peruvian territories by the Armistice of Piura

ledger.note: 1829: Gran Colombia lets the claim go. 'On 10 July 1829, the Armistice of Piura recognised the annexation of Guayaquil to Gran Colombia' and 'recognized Tumbes, Jaen and Maynas as Peruvian territories' (the infobox: 'Implicit Colombian recognition of Peruvian sovereignty'). The Larrea-Gual Treaty of 22 September 1829 ended the war with status quo ante bellum. The land was Peruvian before (/ledger/0 and /ledger/2); Cliopatria adds it to Peru only in 1834. gran-colombia /ledger/8 must become the matching contest_end.

region.text: Guayaquil, held by Peru until 21 July 1829

ledger.note: 1829: Peru leaves Guayaquil. It 'remained under Peruvian occupation until 21 July 1829.'

region.text: Peru, divided into the North Peruvian and South Peruvian states

ledger.note: 1836: Santa Cruz creates the Peru-Bolivian Confederation. 'Santa Cruz decreed the establishment of the Peru-Bolivian Confederation, by decree given in Lima on 28 October 1836'; South Peru (Sicuani assembly, March 1836) and North Peru (constitution 11 August 1836) were its two Peruvian states.
1839: Peru is restored. Santa Cruz 'was defeated in the Battle of Yungay on 20 January 1839, and thus, the Confederation was dissolved' (Gamarra announced the dissolution on 25 August 1839).

region.text: the Chincha Islands (30 km round Pisco, the nearest mainland place in the gazetteer)

ledger.note: 1864: Spain seizes the Chincha Islands. 'In 1864, a Spanish expedition occupied the Chincha Islands.' The Spanish Empire dossier dates it 14 April 1864 from the Chincha Islands War page.

region.text: the Chincha Islands (30 km round Pisco, the nearest mainland place in the gazetteer)

ledger.note: 1866: the Spanish fleet leaves. 'After the battle of Callao on 2 May 1866, the Spanish Navy withdrew from Peru.'

1879: Chile invades Tarapaca. Pisagua was landed on 2 November 1879 and 'the Chilean army captured Iquique ... without resistance'; the battle of Tarapaca (27 November) did not stop the Peruvian retreat to Arica.

1880: Chile holds Moquegua. The page says Chile 'planned to retain' Moquegua, Tacna and Arica until peace terms were met and puts the battle of Los Angeles on 22 March 1880 but gives no occupation date (page silent); mirrors republic-of-chile /ledger/16 (1880, confidence 1) and Cliopatria, which draws Moquegua in Chile's shape 1880-1884.

region.text: the Tarata province (the land in the 1925 shape of republic-of-chile and not in the 1926 shape; the same region as republic-of-chile /ledger/33)

ledger.note: 1880: Chile occupies Tarata. 'Chilean troops occupied Tarata in 1880', during the War of the Pacific, and Chile administered the province 'from 1880 to 1925'; the page gives no month. Mirrors the 1925 return (republic-of-chile /ledger/33).

region.text: the provinces of Tacna and Arica without Tarata, which Chile returned on 1 September 1925

ledger.note: 1880: Chile takes Tacna and Arica. On 26 May 1880 the Chilean army 'destroyed the allied army of 5,150 Bolivians and 8,500 Peruvians' at Tacna; on 7 June 'the last Peruvian bastion in the Tacna Department fell' at Arica. Tarata, inside Tacna, is a separate event (1880, Tarata Province page).
1881: Chile occupies Lima. 'Chilean forces occupied Peru's capital Lima in January 1881' (Chorrillos and Miraflores, 13-15 January).
1883: the Treaty of Ancon ends the Chilean occupation of Tarapaca by cession on 20 October 1883.

1883: Peru cedes Tarapaca. 'Peru formally cede Tarapaca to Chile' in the Treaty of Ancon, 20 October 1883, which also gave Chile Tacna and Arica 'for 10 years', after which 'a plebiscite was to be held'.
1883: Lima is evacuated. 'On 29 October 1883, the Chilean occupation of Lima ended'; the last Chilean troops embarked at Callao on 4 August 1884.

1883: Chile occupies Arequipa. On 29 October 1883 Peruvian troops mutinied against Montero and 'allowed the Chileans to occupy the city'; the page adds that the occupations of Arequipa and Puno 'saw little military action'. republic-of-chile has no matching event yet.

1883: Chile marches on Puno. The page describes a march 'to Arequipa and Puno in October 1883' and 'the occupations of Arequipa and Puno'; it gives no day and no end date, and the extent held round Puno is my reading (60 km). republic-of-chile has no matching event yet.

1884: Chile leaves Moquegua. The page gives no end date for the Moquegua occupation; it is bridged to the last Chilean embarkation, Lynch's forces leaving Callao on 4 August 1884; mirrors republic-of-chile /ledger/29.
1884: Chile leaves Arequipa. The page gives no end date for the occupation of Arequipa; it is bridged to the embarkation of Lynch's forces at Callao on 4 August 1884.
1884: Chile leaves Puno. The page gives no end date for the occupation of Puno; it is bridged to the embarkation of Lynch's forces at Callao on 4 August 1884.

region.text: the Tarata province (the land in the 1925 shape of republic-of-chile and not in the 1926 shape; the same region as republic-of-chile /ledger/33)

ledger.note: 1925: Chile returns Tarata. 'The return of Tarata to Peru on September 1, 1925': Chilean troops occupied the province in 1880 and Chile administered it 'from 1880 to 1925'; Coolidge's mediation 'was significant in the conclusion of the 42-year dispute'. Mirrors republic-of-chile /ledger/33 (a loss there, an end of occupation here, because Peru keeps sovereignty in this dossier). Cliopatria draws the land in Peru's shape from 1926.

1928: Peru gives up Leticia. The Salomon-Lozano Treaty, signed in Lima on 24 March 1922 (Colombia-Peru War page: 'transferred the Leticia district to Colombia'), was approved by the Peruvian Congress on 20 December 1927 and took effect on 19 March 1928; the page says only that the act of transfer was signed in 1930 and gives no handover date. The land is my reading of 'Leticia and other territories' (60 km round Leticia), hence confidence 2; Cliopatria removes it in 1928.

region.text: the provinces of Tacna and Arica without Tarata, which Chile returned on 1 September 1925

ledger.note: 1929: Chile hands Tacna back. The Treaty of Lima of 3 June 1929: 'Tacna was awarded to Peru'; Chile also 'retained its sovereignty over Arica'. Tarata is not in this region: it returned on 1 September 1925 (above). The page gives no date for the physical handover (republic-of-chile dates its occupation_end 1929-08 from another reading); this dossier keeps the treaty date. republic-of-chile /ledger/35 (a 1929 loss of Tacna) should be an occupation_end only, since Peru stayed sovereign here.

1929: Peru gives up Arica. 'Chile ... retained its sovereignty over Arica' by the Treaty of Lima, 3 June 1929; Peru got Tacna, the Tacna-Arica railway administration and a pier at Arica, and up to US$6 million.
1932: Peruvians seize Leticia. 'In the early hours of September 1, 1932, what is now known as the Leticia Incident took place.'

1933: Peru gives Leticia to a League of Nations commission. The war lasted 'to May 24, 1933'; after Sanchez Cerro's death on 30 April, Benavides agreed 'to turn Leticia over to a League of Nations commission'; the Rio de Janeiro Protocol of 1934 reaffirmed the 1922 treaty.

1941: Peru invades Ecuador's coast. 'The Peruvian offensive against Ecuador began on July 23' at Zarumilla; 'by the end of August 1941, Peru occupied the coast: the provinces and cantons of El Oro, Puerto Bolivar'. Ceasefire 31 July 1941.
1941: Peru holds Ecuador's southern mountains. 'In the mountains, the provinces and cantons of Loja and Zamora Chinchipe were occupied.'
1942: Peru leaves El Oro. The Rio Protocol was signed on 29 January 1942 and 'on February 12, 1942, Peruvian troops vacated the Ecuadorian province of El Oro'.

1942: Peru leaves Loja and Zamora Chinchipe. Neither the Ecuadorian-Peruvian War page nor the Rio Protocol page gives a date for the withdrawal from Loja or the Amazon zone (Rio Protocol: signed 29 January 1942, ratified 26 February 1942; 'Peru agreed to withdraw Peruvian military forces from Ecuadorian territory'; the Talara Accord of 2 October 1941 'created a demilitarized zone inside the provinces of El Oro and Loja'; Zamora Chinchipe is not named). February 1942 follows the El Oro withdrawal (page silent: confidence 1).

wars.name: Gran Colombia-Peru War

zones.text: Tumbes, Jaen and Maynas, recognised as Peruvian territories by the Armistice of Piura
Guayaquil, held by Peru until 21 July 1829
Loja (Saraguro, 13 February 1829) and the Cuenca highlands (Portete de Tarqui, 26-27 February 1829)

wars.outcome: Stalemate after Tarqui; the Armistice of Piura (10 July 1829) recognised Tumbes, Jaen and Maynas as Peruvian and Guayaquil as Gran Colombian; the Larrea-Gual Treaty (22 September 1829) restored the status quo ante bellum.
wars.note: Infobox '20 May 1828 - 22 September 1829'; Peru took Guayaquil on 19 January 1829 and left on 21 July.

wars.name: War of the Confederation
wars.outcome: Yungay (20 January 1839) dissolved the Confederation; Peru was restored.
wars.note: The page links to the war but gives no dates for it; Chile's Congress approved the declaration of war on 26 December 1836, the Treaty of Paucarpata was signed on 17 November 1837 and repudiated, and Argentina's Rosas declared war on 19 May 1837.

wars.name: Chincha Islands War

zones.text: the Chincha Islands (30 km round Pisco, the nearest mainland place in the gazetteer)

wars.outcome: Spain withdrew after the battle of Callao on 2 May 1866.
wars.note: The Peru page does not name the war; the Spanish occupation of the Chincha Islands began in 1864.

wars.name: War of the Pacific

zones.text: the provinces of Tacna and Arica

wars.outcome: Chilean victory: Peru ceded Tarapaca by the Treaty of Ancon (20 October 1883) and Tacna and Arica passed to ten years of Chilean control; the plebiscite never took place and the Treaty of Lima (3 June 1929) gave Tacna to Peru and Arica to Chile.

wars.name: Colombia-Peru War
wars.outcome: Status quo ante bellum: Leticia stayed Colombian; the Rio de Janeiro Protocol of 1934 reaffirmed the Salomon-Lozano Treaty.

wars.name: Ecuadorian-Peruvian War
wars.outcome: Peruvian victory; the Rio de Janeiro Protocol of 29 January 1942 followed; Peru left El Oro on 12 February 1942.
wars.note: Combat 5-31 July 1941 (infobox); the Talara Accord of 2 October 1941 set a demilitarised zone.

wars.name: Cenepa War
wars.outcome: The border dispute 'not entirely resolved until the Cenepa War of 1995'; the Brasilia Presidential Act of 26 October 1998 was the 'definitive peace agreement'.
wars.note: No territory changed hands on the pages opened; 78 km of the border stayed unmarked for fifty years after 1942.

certainty.note: The Amazon frontiers with Gran Colombia/Ecuador, Brazil and Bolivia were unsurveyed; the 1829 treaty left the line with Gran Colombia to a commission. The Tarapaca line is sharp from the Treaty of Ancon (20 October 1883).

The Tacna-Arica line was unsettled until 1929; the Tarapaca line (1883) is sharp; the Brazil line is partly fixed by the 1909 Treaty of Rio de Janeiro and the Colombian line by the 1922 Salomon-Lozano treaty.
The Chilean line is the 1929 Treaty of Lima and the Colombian line the 1922/1934 treaties; the Ecuadorian line is the exception, 'some 78 km ... left unmarked' under the 1942 Rio Protocol until 1998.
All frontiers settled; the Ecuador line by the Brasilia Presidential Act of 26 October 1998.

notes:
REVISED 2026-10-19 after the adversarial review (fail). Changes: (a) 1821-1824 is now the coast and the north (Tumbes, Piura, Lambayeque, La Libertad, Cajamarca, Amazonas, Ancash, Lima, Ica; Protectorate of Peru page), not a circle round Lima; the 1824-12 gain is the remainder. (b) Tumbes, Jaen and Maynas are Peruvian throughout and contested with gran-colombia from 1822 to the Armistice of Piura (10 July 1829); the 1829 gain became a contest_end, keyframes 1825 and 1828 are adjust, the redundant 1829 keyframe is removed. (c) Tarata: occupation_end 1925-09 and the 1929 end narrowed to the rest of Tacna and Arica. (d) Chilean occupations of Moquegua, Arequipa and Puno added. (e) Callao dated 23 January 1826 (confidence 3); Leticia 19 March 1928 (confidence 2).
Cliopatria rows and how they are used: (1) the 1822 shape (1.47 M km2) draws nearly all of Peru, Peru-claimed Brazilian Amazon (1,211 cells, lost to Cliopatria's Bolivia shape in 1825) and Tarapaca/Arica; the dossier reduces 1821-1824 to the coast and north (about 0.25 M km2). The page names no department, so the nine are my reading (north confidence 2, Lima 3). Not drawn for want of dated pages: the royalist Ica incursion (April 1822), the defeat at Torata and Moquegua (January 1823), the royalist re-entry into Lima (25 February 1824, after the Callao mutiny of 5 February) and Bolivar's arrival (10 December 1823). (2) Tacna and Arica (1880-1929) and the other Chilean-occupied land (Moquegua, Arequipa, Puno, parts of Lima and Ica in Cliopatria's 1880-1884 shape) are kept inside Peru's shapes with occupation events, because the Treaty of Ancon gave Chile only 'temporary control' (War of the Pacific page); Cliopatria gives them to Chile. republic-of-chile should record occupation events: it has Tarapaca 1879, Moquegua 1880-1884, Tacna and Arica 1880 (its /ledger/34 is 1929-08, Peru has 1929-06, the page gives only the 3 June signing) and Tarata 1925, but no Arequipa or Puno, and its /ledger/35 records a 1929 loss of Tacna that should be an occupation_end only. (3) The 1836-1839 gap is the Peru-Bolivian Confederation row (peru-bolivian-confederation, another group); Peru is recorded as a loss on 28 October 1836 and a gain after Yungay. (4) The 1825 Brazilian-Amazon loss (1,217 of 1,230 cells go to Cliopatria's Bolivia shape) and the 1853 loss of 29 Brazilian cells are not explained by any page: Brazil-Peru border (1909 treaty only), Bolivia-Peru relations and Brazil-Peru relations are silent, Bolivia-Peru border and the 1851 treaty page returned 404; the one-cell blip of 1950 likewise. (5) Leticia: signed 24 March 1922, approved by the Peruvian Congress 20 December 1927, effective 19 March 1928 (Salomon-Lozano page), act of transfer 1930, handover date not on the page; the loss is at 1928-03, confidence 2. (6) The Rio Protocol (29 January 1942) changed no cells of the Peru shape; neither it nor the war page dates the withdrawal from Loja and Zamora Chinchipe (confidence 1). (7) No rulers: the pages opened give no list. (8) Gazetteer: all names resolved; 'Maynas' is drawn as Loreto, 'Jaen' as a radius. (9) The Protectorate (San Martin, decree of 3 August 1821; page infobox 28 July 1821 - 20 September 1822) is not recorded as a rename. (10) Counterparts: gran-colombia, republic-of-chile, republic-of-colombia, republic-of-ecuador, spanish-empire, peru-bolivian-confederation, bolivia all have rows or are owned by another group. Mirrors still to be made elsewhere: spanish-empire (widen the 1821-07 loss to the coast and north), gran-colombia (/ledger/4 gain -> contest_start, /ledger/8 loss -> contest_end, keyframe 2 adjust), republic-of-chile (Arequipa, Puno; /ledger/35).
